summary:
Amazonas stands under Colombia's national framework, which is among the most developed in Latin America on legal gender recognition. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments; the official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025.

The national framework sits alongside lethal violence. On 5 April 2025 a video showed Sara Millerey, 32, beaten in Bello, Antioquia, thrown into a creek and unable to swim with fractured limbs; she died the following afternoon and no one has been arrested. Thirteen trans people were killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, and the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025. More than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023. Her death provoked national outrage and mobilisations against transphobia.

Some of the targeting is organised. In Guajira, armed groups have circulated flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". In Caquetá, armed groups gave trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed and circulated "social cleansing" flyers against trans women; trans salon owners in the department have been forced to move after death threats, and trans women there have few options beyond sex work. An activist quoted in reporting says the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording the killings as ordinary cases. Killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case, described in reporting as calculated brutality persisting amid the country's decades-long civil conflict.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Couples married abroad involving a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

Access to facilities and custody are covered by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

Amazonas state policy has included discrimination based on gender identity since 2006. Since the March 2018 unanimous Supreme Federal Court ruling, transgender people may change legal gender at a registry post without surgery, hormonal therapy, judicial authorization or medical report, with registry-office gender changes reported up 59% by 2024. Amazonas has no specific law recognizing non-binary gender; in 2022 Álex Souza de Sá became the first non-binary person recognized, requiring rectification in Rio de Janeiro and six months of insistence plus intervention by the Public Defender's Office to obtain recognition in Manaus where the registry lacked a gender-neutral marker.

For facilities, on 18 October 2022 the mayor of Manaus signed a law banning unisex restrooms in the city. For care, in November 2023 the State Public Defender's Office opened monitoring of public health services for transgender and travesti people including hormones and surgeries, in August 2024 the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office recommended the state formally enable outpatient and hospital transsexualization services including sexual reassignment surgeries with deadlines for submission to the Ministry of Health, and on 10 June 2025 Governor Wilson Lima signed Law No. 7,552 banning gender-affirming care for minors under 18.

For protection machinery, in 2021 the State Public Defender's Office created the Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship Working Group focused on human rights violations and training security agents, and in August 2024 the State Court of Justice released the booklet Home is a Right! for LGBTQ youth expelled from homes stating conversion therapies are "prohibited and ineffective." Cases of violence against LGBTQ people in the state are described as underreported, with 43 cases registered according to Brazilian Public Security Forum data cited in research.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1830 when the Imperial Penal Code removed all references to sodomy. Same-sex marriage has been legal in Amazonas since 2013 via National Council of Justice decision following the 2011 Supreme Federal Court decision, with a 328% increase between 2020 and 2025, 287 unions registered in 2024 and 98 in the first five months of 2025. Same-sex adoption was first authorized in Amazonas in November 2012 by a state court judge, with nationwide legalization by the Supreme Federal Court in 2015. Since 2006 state policies include discrimination based on sexual orientation, and since 2019 homophobia has been criminalized nationwide as equivalent to racism.

Assembly and expression restrictions include State Law 6,469/2023 prohibiting participation of children and adolescents in pride parades with fines up to R$10,000, and the 17 October 2024 law prohibiting reproduction of digital media using children linked to homosexuality, amended on 13 December 2025 to remove the term homosexuality and prohibit reproduction of sexual content linked to children in cultural and artistic media. On 5 July 2025 Fernando Vilaça de Souza was beaten and killed in Manaus after reacting to homophobic insults, with prior bullying reported by area residents.
tangentialFactors:
Amazonas led North and Central-West states with 4.66 LGBTQIA+ persons murdered per million inhabitants in 2018, a per-capita figure rather than a raw count.

Amazonas State Law No. 6,463 of 10 October 2023 expressly prohibits use of neutral language, non-binary dialect, or any expression departing from standard Portuguese in curricula and teaching materials of public and private educational institutions and in official documents of schools and public agencies statewide. This restricts how a visitor's gender marker or identity may be recorded or discussed in official and educational settings.

On 23 May 2019 a majority of Brazil's Supreme Federal Tribunal (6 of 11 justices) voted to criminalize transphobia under Brazil's 1989 racism law punishable by up to five years' imprisonment until Congress enacts specific LGBT-discrimination legislation, to take effect after all justices voted on 5 June 2019. This is the national basis on which Amazonas's 2019 transphobia criminalization rests.
localsOnly:
Amazonas residents benefit from the State Public Defender's Office's permanent Working Group on Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship, created 28 June 2021, which identifies LGBTQIA+ human-rights violations in public security, trains public-security agents, and issues recommendations and extrajudicial measures. LGBTQIA+ victims in Manaus can obtain assistance via Disk 129 Monday-Friday 8am-2pm through the Specialized Human Rights unit.

As of 1 November 2023 the State Public Defender's health unit opened a collective procedure to audit SUS care for trans people covering access to hormonization, outpatient services, and lack of accreditation for gender-affirming surgeries including sexual reassignment. In October 2023 the Manaus Municipal Health Secretariat committed to dispense standardized medications to trans people on prescription from the Codajás Outpatient Clinic that handles hormonization and to designate reference UBS primary-care units in each city zone, while the State Health Secretariat was ordered to report on equitable integral care including remedying hormoniotherapy gaps guaranteed under Federal Council of Medicine Resolution No. 2,265 of 2019.

In August 2024 the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office recommended that the state of Amazonas guarantee integral health care to the LGBTQIAPN+ population, including trans people. On 10 June 2025 Governor Wilson Lima signed Law No. 7,552 banning gender-affirming care for minors under 18.

In Amazonas as of August 2024, LGBTQIAPN+ adolescents facing family discrimination and expulsion are guaranteed under ECA Article 17 physical, psychological and moral integrity including identity and autonomy, with bullying criminalized under Law 14.811/2024 by fine to 4 years' imprisonment, homophobia criminalized per 2019 STF ruling as imprescriptible and non-bailable, conversion/"gay cure" therapy prohibited as illegal and ineffective, and legal support available through the Defensoria Especializada em Direitos Humanos.

During 2021-2022 in Amazonas, crimes involving transsexual persons formed part of only 0.36% of total reported crimes in the capital and interior, police occurrence reports did not identify transfobia or gender, sexuality, race and intersectionality markers, trans victim data were few and badly structured with victims not infrequently inverted to accused through faulty BOs, and unprepared public agents and defective registration mechanisms left trans subjects invisibilized and without protection.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory contains a substantial contamination problem: claim [3] and several supporting claims ([4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9], [10], [11], [12]) describe Amazonas as a state of Brazil, citing Brazilian institutions (Supreme Federal Court, Public Defender's Office of Amazonas state in Brazil, Manaus as a Brazilian city, Governor Wilson Lima, Brazilian reais, the Brazilian Public Security Forum, SUS, the Imperial Penal Code of 1830). Amazonas is also a department of Colombia. Whether these claims pertain to the Colombian department or the Brazilian state is unresolved from the inventory; the Brazilian-institution citations indicate the former, but the jurisdiction label is ambiguous. This should be verified before publication.

Claims [1] and [2] explicitly state the sources contain no information on Amazonas; their content is national Colombian or Caquetá-specific and is carried by the parent record.

The inventory does not resolve whether the Colombian department of Amazonas has any region-specific laws, incidents, or institutions distinct from Colombia's national framework. No region-specific Colombian signal was identified.
